title: Versailles Takes Shape
summary: On June 23, 1792—weeks after Kentucky’s statehood—the legislature seated Woodford County’s courts at Versailles, a name chosen to honor Lafayette.
bodyMarkdown:
Versailles began as a courthouse problem. When Virginia's General Assembly carved [Woodford County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Woodford_County,_Kentucky) out of Fayette County in 1788, the ninth and last county Virginia created in the District of Kentucky, the new county had justices but no town. Beginning in 1789, its first court sessions met in the home of Judge Caleb Wallace while settlers argued over where a permanent seat should go.

The answer came on June 23, 1792, only weeks after Kentucky became a state on June 1, 1792. The town was laid out on about 80 acres at a place locals called Falling Spring. The land belonged to Hezekiah Briscoe, who was still a child, so the decisions fell to his guardian, Marquis Calmes, a major in the Revolutionary War.

Calmes chose the name. He called the town [Versailles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Versailles,_Kentucky) after the French royal seat, honoring the [Marquis de Lafayette](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gilbert_du_Motier,_Marquis_de_Lafayette), whom sources describe as a family friend. The choice fit the moment: Kentuckians of the 1790s widely remembered France as the ally that helped win independence, and [Louisville](https://grokipedia.com/page/Louisville,_Kentucky) had been named for Louis XVI for the same reason.

A county seat needed a courthouse. A log building by Jesse Graddy, reportedly built for $22.50, was replaced by a stone courthouse completed in 1794.

Farming gave the young town its living. Tobacco became an early staple and hemp was grown alongside it, much of it sent to markets in Lexington, and the Pepper family began distilling on Glenns Creek; the distillery now known as Woodford Reserve took shape under Oscar Pepper around 1838. Even so, Versailles was not incorporated as a town until 1837, more than four decades after it was laid out.

One thing never took root: the French pronunciation. Locals say vər-SAYLZ, a small, lasting sign that the name was borrowed for its meaning rather than its sound.

## Kentucky today

Versailles remains the seat of Woodford County, about 13 miles west of Lexington, with about 10,600 residents in a 2024 estimate, according to [Grokipedia's Versailles article](https://grokipedia.com/page/Versailles,_Kentucky). The Pepper distillery on Glenns Creek, now Woodford Reserve, is a National Historic Landmark, and people visiting it still take the roads that once carried court-day traffic into town.
